    Guide
    
  
    How to use Search Studio
    
  
    Three places matter: the library, where you learn an algorithm; the studio, where you run it; and the export panel, where you take the trace away.
    

  
    1. Learn the algorithm first
    
  
    Open the library and pick an algorithm. Its page has:
    
  
      
    
    • Introduction in plain language, and a precise definition.
      • 
    
    • Pseudocode with a sentence on what each line does and why.
      • 
    
    • Formulas: each written out, read aloud in words, and justified.
      • 
    
    • Properties (complete? optimal? time and space) and common traps.
      • 
  
    
  
    Press Try it to open the studio with that algorithm and a suitable example already loaded.
    

  
    2. Run it in the studio
    
  
    Choose a problem
    
  
      
    
    • Examples come with the site: the six-city instance from the TSP deck, two five-city practice matrices, and three graphs for uninformed and informed search.
      • 
    
    • Random makes a new TSP or graph from a size and a seed. The same seed always gives the same problem, so you can share it.
      • 
    
    • Edit shows the problem as text you can change (format below) and saves it under My problems in this browser.
      • 
    
    • Import accepts a problem as JSON (paste it or choose a file); Export problem gives you that JSON back.
      • 
  
    
  
    Choose an algorithm and its settings
    
  
    Only algorithms that fit the problem type are listed. Settings such as start city, beam width, tabu tenure, temperature or random seed appear below. Changing anything re-runs the algorithm from the start.
    
  
    Step through
    
  
      
    
    • ← → step back and forward, Space plays or pauses, Home / End jump to the first or last step.
      • 
    
    • The slider scrubs; the speed menu sets seconds per step.
      • 
    
    • The Trace tab lists every step's caption; click one to jump to it.
      • 
  
    

  
    3. Read the stage
    
  
    Left: the graph. Right: the working table for this algorithm, with the current row highlighted, and a small chart where one helps (temperature runs, restarts, roulette wheels). Below: the lists, such as OPEN and CLOSED written as node pairs (node, parent, value). At the bottom, in yellow, one sentence says what just happened.
    
  
    
    
    you seeit means
    
    
      
    yellow ringthe node being expanded or the city the tour is at
    
      
    orange ringon OPEN (generated, waiting), or a candidate being considered
    
      
    grey nodeon CLOSED (already expanded)
    
      
    greenpath found, accepted edge, optimum, goal (double ring)
    
      
    red dashesan edge being removed or a choice being rejected
    
      
    orange dashescandidate edges from the current city
    
      
    blue dashesthe second parent tour, or an out-and-back trip in the savings heuristic
    
      
    thick orange edges (ACO)pheromone: thicker means more
    
        
  
    

  
    4. Problem text formats
    
  
    TSP: names, then the matrix
    

    A B C D E
0 58 92 34 81
58 0 20 46 70
92 20 0 28 53
34 46 28 0 12
81 70 53 12 0
    
  
    Use any whitespace or commas. The matrix may be asymmetric; the site tells you when it is.
    
  
    Graph: start, goal, heuristic, edges
    

    start S
goal G
undirected
h S 7
h A 5
# edges: from to cost
S A 2
S B 5
A G 6
B G 1
    
  
    Write directed instead of undirected for one-way edges. Lines starting with # are comments. Nodes without a position are placed on a circle.
    

  
    5. Take it away
    
  
      
    
    • Printable trace: a self-contained HTML page with a cover (problem, settings, pseudocode) and one step per printed page. Open it in a browser and print, or save as PDF.
      • 
    
    • Trace JSON / CSV: every step's caption, table and lists, for notes or spreadsheets.
      • 
    
    • Current step as SVG: the graph drawing, for slides.
      • 
  
    

  
    Conventions used everywhere
    
  
      
    
    • Ties are broken alphabetically unless a setting says otherwise; MoveGen lists neighbours alphabetically.
      • 
    
    • Tours are written in path representation; the edge back to the start is always included in the cost.
      • 
    
    • Graph search is graph search: a node already on OPEN or CLOSED is not added again; UCS and A* update it when they find a cheaper path.
      • 
    
    • The goal test happens when a node is picked from OPEN, as in the course.
      • 
    
    • Random choices use a seeded generator, so a run can always be repeated exactly.
      • 
  
    

    

    
  
    
  
    About
    
  
    About Search Studio
    
  
    A study companion for search methods: the algorithms of state-space search, informed search and stochastic optimisation, traced exactly the way they are traced by hand.
    
  
    Why it exists
    
  
    Search algorithms are easy to describe and surprisingly easy to trace wrongly: a missed tie-break, a child added twice, a forgotten closing edge, a savings pair merged that should have been refused. Seeing every step, with the working table and the OPEN and CLOSED lists side by side, makes those mistakes visible.
    
  
    What it covers
    
  
      
    
    • State-space search: Breadth First, Depth First, Depth First Iterative Deepening, Uniform Cost, Best First and A* (with weighted A*).
      • 
    
    • Travelling salesperson, constructive: Nearest Neighbour, Greedy, Savings, and brute force as the exact reference.
      • 
    
    • Perturbation and local search: 2-city exchange, 2-edge exchange, Or-opt, 3-edge exchange, Variable Neighbourhood Descent, Beam Search, Tabu Search, Iterated Hill Climbing, Random Walk, Simulated Annealing.
      • 
    
    • Population methods: Genetic Algorithm with cycle, PMX, order, alternating-edges, heuristic and ordinal crossover, and Ant Colony Optimisation.
      • 
  
    
  
    Notation
    
  
    The site follows the notation of AI: Search Methods for Problem Solving (Prof. Deepak Khemani, IIT Madras) and his book A First Course in Artificial Intelligence: MoveGen and GoalTest, OPEN and CLOSED as lists of node pairs, path representation for tours, the sigmoid acceptance rule for simulated annealing, and the course's crossover conventions. It is an independent study aid and is not affiliated with or endorsed by IIT Madras.
    
  
    How results are checked
    
  
    Every algorithm is run against every example and against random problems on each build. Tours must be permutations whose reported cost matches a recomputation; paths must run from start to goal with the reported cost. On the six-city instance the results are compared with an independent Python implementation (optimum 224, Nearest Neighbour 264, Greedy 238, Savings 224, and so on).
    
  
    Further reading
    
  
      
    
    • Deepak Khemani, A First Course in Artificial Intelligence, McGraw Hill Education.
      • 
    
    • D. S. Johnson and L. A. McGeoch, “The Traveling Salesman Problem: A Case Study in Local Optimization”, in Local Search in Combinatorial Optimization (1997): how far above optimal the classic TSP heuristics land in practice.
      • 
    
    • M. Dorigo and T. Stützle, Ant Colony Optimization, MIT Press (2004).
      • 
  
    

    

    
  
    
  
    Contribute
    
  
    Add an algorithm or an example
    
  
    The library is the algorithms/ folder. Add a file, run the build, and it appears on the site with its own learn page and studio entry.
    

  
    Project layout
    

    search-studio/
├── algorithms/          one file per algorithm, grouped by family
│   ├── _template.js     copy this to start (files starting with _ are skipped)
│   ├── search/          bfs.js, dfs.js, dfid.js, ucs.js, best-first.js, a-star.js
│   └── tsp/             nearest-neighbour.js, greedy.js, savings.js, …
├── examples/            one JSON file per built-in problem
├── src/
│   ├── core/            registry, problem model, search engine, TSP helpers
│   ├── ui/              stage renderer and the app
│   ├── pages/           home, guide, about, contribute (plain HTML)
│   └── styles/          studio.css
├── tools/
│   ├── build.mjs        scans the folders and builds the site
│   └── test.mjs         runs every algorithm on every example
├── index.html           generated: the site, loading files from the folders
└── dist/search-studio.html   generated: the whole site in one file
    

  
    Add an algorithm in four steps
    
  
      
    
    1. Copy algorithms/_template.js to algorithms/<family>/<name>.js.
      2. 
    
    2. Fill in the metadata (id, name, family, problem), the learn block and run.
      3. 
    
    3. Run node tools/build.mjs. The build loads every file, checks that it registers, runs it on the examples, and regenerates index.html, the manifest and the single-file build. Use node tools/build.mjs --watch while you work.
      4. 
    
    4. Open index.html (or serve the folder with npx serve) and find your algorithm in the library.
      5. 
  
    

  
    The algorithm file
    

    Studio.register({
  id: "tsp-my-method",            // unique, used in links: #algo-tsp-my-method
  name: "My method",
  family: "TSP · local search",   // the library groups by this
  problem: "tsp",                 // tsp, graph, game, andor, planning, rules, csp, linedrawing, circuit, alignment
  week: 3,                        // course week 1–11: places it on the course map
  order: 200,                     // position inside the family
  summary: "One sentence for the library card.",
  pseudocode: `...`,
  complexity: "O(n²) per step",
  learn: {
    intro: "Plain-language introduction.",
    definition: "Precise definition.",
    steps: [["pseudocode line", "what it does and why"]],
    formulas: [{ f: "formula", read: "in words", why: "why it holds" }],
    why: "When it works and when it fails.",
    traps: ["Common mistake"],
    props: { complete: "no", optimal: "no", time: "…", space: "…" }
  },
  params: [
    { key: "start", label: "Start city", type: "city", default: P => P.ids[0] },
    { key: "w", label: "Beam width", type: "int", default: 2 },
    Studio.seedParam(1)
  ],
  run(P, params) {
    // P.ids, P.d(a, b), P.cost(tour) for TSP; P.adj, P.h, P.start, P.goal for graphs
    return { steps: [ /* one object per snapshot */ ], result: { tour, cost } };
  }
});
    

  
    What a step can contain
    
  
    
    
    fieldshapeshown as
    
    
      
    captionstringthe yellow sentence under the stage (required)
    
      
    nodes{ A: { state, badge } }node colours; states: plain, current, open, closed, visited, path, goal, start
    
      
    edges[{ u, v, state, label }]edges; states: faint, tour, path, candidate, added, removed, rejected, alt, tree, pheromone
    
      
    table{ title, columns, rows, rowStates }the working table; row states: ok, bad, warn, cur, dim
    
      
    lists[{ label, items: [{ text, state }] }]OPEN / CLOSED style rows
    
      
    stats[{ label, value, state }]small figures under the graph
    
      
    chart{ kind: "walk" | "drops" | "bars" | "pie", … }a small chart beside the table
    
        
  
    
  
    Helpers in src/core do most of the work: Studio.search.run for OPEN/CLOSED searches, Studio.tsp.moveGens for 2-city, 2-edge, Or-opt and 3-edge neighbourhoods, Studio.tspSteps.hillClimb for traced hill climbing, Studio.tsp.crossovers for every crossover, and Studio.rng(seed) for repeatable randomness.
    

  
    Add an example problem
    
  
    Drop a JSON file into examples/ and rebuild. In the studio, Export problem gives you a file in exactly this shape.
    

    { "id": "graph-my-maze", "type": "graph", "name": "My maze",
  "note": "One line shown under the problem selector.",
  "nodes": [{ "id": "S", "x": 0, "y": 0, "h": 4 }, …],
  "edges": [["S", "A", 2], …], "start": "S", "goal": "G", "directed": false }

{ "id": "tsp-my-cities", "type": "tsp", "name": "My cities",
  "cities": [{ "id": "A", "x": 1, "y": 2 }, …],
  "matrix": [[0, 12, …], …] }          // optional: without it, 10 × Euclidean distance
    

  
    Checklist before you share
    
  
      
    
    • node tools/test.mjs passes: every step has a caption, edges and nodes exist, tours are permutations with correct costs.
      • 
    
    • Ties are broken the course's way (alphabetically) or a setting says otherwise.
      • 
    
    • The learn block explains every formula you use and at least one trap.
      • 
    
    • Random choices go through Studio.rng(seed) so runs repeat exactly.
      •
